claim: For pure qubit states, maximal Entanglement Distance does not by itself constrain the quantum Fisher information for a prescribed common phase generator. With \(J_z=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i\), every even \(N\ge2\) has states with the same maximal value \(E_{\mathrm D}=N\) but endpoint QFI values \(F_Q=0\) and \(F_Q=N^2\): a tensor product of singlets gives the first and an \(N\)-qubit GHZ state gives the second. Already for \(N=2\), the maximally entangled family \((I\otimes R_y(\theta))|\Phi^+\rangle\) has \(E_{\mathrm D}=2\) for all \(\theta\) while \(F_Q[J_z]=2(1+\cos\theta)\), so the full allowed interval \([0,4]\) occurs at one fixed maximal Entanglement Distance. Thus the trace-over-local-directions QFI/Entanglement-Distance identity should not be read as a generator-specific certificate of Heisenberg scaling for a prescribed collective sensing Hamiltonian.

correctness.rationale: The proof was reconstructed from the Entanglement-Distance linear-entropy formula and the pure-state QFI variance identity. The two-qubit Bell orbit gives \(F_Q=2(1+\cos\theta)\) by a direct Pauli calculation. Tensor-product singlets and GHZ states give the all-even-N endpoints. The numerical verifier only checks finite instances and is not used to infer the general statements.

value.rationale: The result gives a sharp structural boundary for a new metrological interpretation rather than a routine restatement: it shows exactly what information a scalar trace-over-local-directions entanglement quantity loses for a prescribed sensing Hamiltonian. The two-qubit construction saturates the complete QFI interval, and the all-even-N examples attain both zero and Heisenberg endpoints at identical maximal Entanglement Distance.
